title: Urinary system: kidneys to urethra
note: Kidney has a Greek root (nephr/o) and a Latin one (ren/o); bladder is cyst/o or vesic/o. The suffix -uria means urine or urination. Do not confuse pyel/o (renal pelvis) with py/o (pus), or ureter/o (kidney to bladder) with urethr/o (bladder to outside).

read.title: Filter, funnel, store, release
text: The urinary system makes, carries and stores urine. Each kidney (nephr/o, ren/o) holds about a million nephrons, its functional units. At the start of each nephron a glomerulus, a tuft of capillaries, filters the blood; the tubules then reclaim water and useful substances and leave wastes behind. Urine collects in the renal pelvis (pyel/o), drains down a ureter (ureter/o) to the bladder (cyst/o, vesic/o), and leaves through the urethra (urethr/o).

Two spelling traps deserve attention. Ureter and urethra are different tubes: there are two ureters, one from each kidney, but only one urethra. And pyel/o, the renal pelvis, is not py/o, pus, so pyelonephritis involves the kidney while pyuria means pus in the urine.

Many urinary terms end in -uria. Put a word part in front to say what is unusual: anuria is no urine, oliguria is scanty urine, nocturia is excessive urination at night, and hematuria is blood in the urine. Procedure terms reuse familiar suffixes: cystoscopy views the bladder and nephrectomy removes a kidney.
